messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Jamal had spent most of his life in motion, first on dance stages in Chicago and later teaching a small class at a community arts studio in his neighborhood, but after the crash his body and the world around him felt altered in a way he could not explain away. The collision happened on a winter evening when a delivery van ran a red light and struck the driver’s side of the car while he was turning out of a lot near a busy intersection. He remembered the metal lurching, the sound of glass and horns, and then a strange discontinuity in the rest of it, as if the minutes after impact had been broken into fragments he could not put back together. Since then, when he tries to tell the story, Jamal can only offer pieces: the steering wheel twisted against him, someone speaking through a window, the smell of coolant and smoke, his own hand reaching for a seatbelt that seemed suddenly impossible to trust. The rest feels missing, and when he deliberately tries to summon the full sequence, it slips away from him. That incomplete memory has left him with no clear account even in his own mind, and he has come to doubt himself in a deeper way, wondering whether he will ever do the right thing if something dangerous happens again. He is also haunted by the sense that the people and institutions that should have protected him failed him, because traffic lights, other drivers, and the systems meant to keep the road safe had not stopped the van from hitting him. What frightens him most is how unreliable his own body now feels to him; since the injury, he has been certain that it might betray him again without warning, and that belief has made him watchful about every small change in how he moves or breathes.

In the weeks after the collision, those convictions narrowed his life. Jamal began avoiding going out whenever he could, arranging groceries and errands around the quietest times or asking others to do them, because leaving the apartment felt like stepping back into a place where another sudden impact could happen. He also pulled away from people he had known before the event, especially former students and fellow dancers he used to see regularly, because their questions and their sympathy made him feel exposed and because he could not bear the possibility that they would notice how uncertain he now felt. In therapy he found himself doing something similar, steering away from discussion of the crash whenever the conversation came close to the parts he could not piece together, almost as if not looking too directly might spare him from the shame of not being able to explain it. These habits were not random to him; they made sense because he no longer trusted his judgment or his body, and because he feared that if he let himself dwell on the event he would be flooded by what he could not control. Yet the more he kept himself from the outside world, the more the world seemed dangerous. He became tense in public spaces, needing to sit with his back against a wall so he could see the room, and when something took longer than expected—a bus that did not arrive, a delayed return call from the mechanic, a pause in the street outside his building—he automatically assumed something bad was happening. Unexpected or loud sounds, especially a sharp brake squeal or a slammed door, left him instantly on high alert. Those moments then pushed him back into his avoidance, making him less willing to go out again and more determined to keep contact with people to a minimum.

Jamal also noticed that the gaps in his memory fed the same spiral. Because the crash lives in fragments, he keeps scanning for signs that he is missing something important, and that uncertainty intensifies his sense that danger could be present before he can name it. The broken recall also deepens his self-doubt: if he cannot even tell a clear story of what happened, he reasons, how can he trust his own understanding now? That uncertainty spills into everyday situations, where he hesitates before decisions that once would have felt automatic, and then avoids the situation altogether because he is afraid of choosing badly. His mistrust of his body works in the same way. A small ache, a sudden stiffness, or a momentary shortness of breath can make him feel that something is wrong, and once that alarm is raised he monitors everything around him more closely, listening for noises and positioning himself for escape. In that way his effort to stay safe has begun to keep his threat system permanently switched on. Months after the crash, he has found himself teaching less at the studio, refusing invitations from old friends, and spending much of the day inside his apartment where he can control the furniture and the angle of his chair. He has come for help now because the life he built around movement and connection has become smaller and smaller, and because he is tired of living as though every delay, every sound, and every uncertain sensation means the danger is back. He is most afraid that he will remain trapped in this watchfulness forever, but he still hopes that if he can make sense of what happened, he may learn how to trust himself enough to move through the world again.
